1000021.etyen:
Internationalism, based on the European name tradition represented by Latin Aegyptus (“Egypt”), itself from Ancient Greek Αἴγυπτος (Aíguptos, “Egypt”), ultimately from Egyptian ḥwt-kꜣ-ptḥ (“house of the ka of Ptah”). The Egyptian name is formed from ḥwt (“enclosure, temple”), kꜣ (“ka”) and ptḥ (“Ptah”), referring to the temple of Ptah at Memphis.
Parallel international adaptations include Danish Egypten, Swedish Egypten, German Ägypten, Dutch Egypte, English Egypt and French Égypte (“Egypt”).

1000533.etyen:
Borrowed from Latin Terra (“the Earth; Terra, the personified Earth”), from Latin terra (“earth, land, ground”), from Proto-Italic Proto-Italic *tersā, from Proto-Indo-European Proto-Indo-European *ters-eh₂, from *ters- (“to dry”). The Latin noun originally referred to the “dry [land]”, in contrast to water or the sky.
The astronomical use continues the Latin name for the Earth. The mythological use reflects the personification of the earth as a divine figure, especially Latin Terra Mater (“Mother Earth”), closely identified with Tellūs (“Tellus”).

1005141.etyen:
Univerbation of Gud (“God”) + skje (“to be accorded”) + takk (“thanks”), from the expression gud skje takk, literally “thanks be to God”. Here skje retains the older sense “be accorded, fall to”.
The first element continues Old Norse guð (“God, god”), also goð, from Proto-Germanic *gudą (“god”); its further origin is disputed. The verb derives from Middle Low German schēn (“to happen”), ultimately from Proto-Germanic *skehaną (“to move quickly; happen”), from Proto-Indo-European *skek- (“to move quickly, jump”). The final element continues Old Norse þǫkk (“thanks, gratitude”), from Proto-Germa
